drapeaux.note: Langue d'origine : français ; auteur : François Truffaut (Une certaine tendance du cinéma français, 1954).

titre: What Truffaut called a policy, America turned into a theory
accroche: In 1954, a twenty-one-year-old critic tore into French cinema in *Cahiers du cinéma*. Eight years later, an American turned his position into a system.
contenu_vulgarise:
In January 1954, a young critic of twenty-one publishes fifteen pages in issue 31 of *Cahiers du cinéma*. He is living at the home of André Bazin, his mentor, who co-edits the magazine with Jacques Doniol-Valcroze. The two men had first rejected an earlier version of the text, titled *Le Temps du mépris* (The Time of Contempt), judged too insulting to the champions of French cinema. François Truffaut reworks it, removes some of the personal attacks, and backs it with a concrete demonstration: he borrows a screenplay from his two main targets, Jean Aurenche and Pierre Bost, to show, by example, what he holds against them.

## Screenwriters, not auteurs

The text, *Une certaine tendance du cinéma français* (A Certain Tendency of the French Cinema), takes aim at what Truffaut calls the Tradition of Quality: polished literary adaptations, faithful to the spirit of the works according to their makers, but written entirely by the same screenwriters before a director comes along to add camera setups. Truffaut sets against them a handful of filmmakers who write their own dialogue or invent their own stories: Jean Renoir, Robert Bresson, Jean Cocteau, Jacques Becker, Abel Gance, Max Ophüls, Jacques Tati, Roger Leenhardt. His conclusion fits in a single sentence: he cannot believe in the peaceful coexistence of the Tradition of Quality and a cinema of auteurs. The following year, he christens this position the *politique des auteurs* (the “auteurs policy”), an editorial policy embraced by a handful of young critics at *Cahiers*, not a general aesthetic theory.

## What it shifts

It is an American critic, Andrew Sarris, who eight years later, in the winter 1962 issue of *Film Culture*, translates and systematizes this policy in a text titled “Notes on the Auteur Theory in 1962.” In passing from one language to the other, the editorial policy of a small French magazine becomes a theory in the full sense, a system meant to apply to any filmmaker in any country, which Truffaut never claimed to have written: he was not drawing up a universal grid for reading films, he was defending a handful of specific filmmakers against a handful of specific screenwriters, in the narrow context of French cinema in 1954. The American critic Pauline Kael will sharply attack this hardened version, arguing that a film remains a collective work, never the work of one man alone, even one credited as director. There is one last irony in this founding text: when he wrote it, Truffaut had not yet directed a single film. He makes his first feature only five years later, with *Les Quatre Cents Coups* (The 400 Blows), after two short films, *Une Visite* (A Visit, 1955) and *Les Mistons* (The Mischief Makers, 1957); he thus finds himself having to embody the figure of the auteur that he had just invented on paper.

carte.punch: Truffaut was talking about an editorial policy. The United States turned it into a universal theory.
carte.idee: In January 1954, Truffaut attacks the screenwriters who dominate French cinema in *Cahiers du cinéma*, and the following year christens his position the *politique des auteurs*. In 1962, the American Andrew Sarris translates it into a general theory, more rigid than the original intent.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: *Une certaine tendance du cinéma français*, full text
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The 1954 article in its entirety, to follow Truffaut's complete argument against the Tradition of Quality.

quiz.question: What did the “politique des auteurs” formulated by Truffaut in 1954-1955 actually stand for, before it became “auteur theory” in the United States?
choix: A universal aesthetic theory, meant to apply to any filmmaker, in any country
An editorial stance, defending a handful of filmmakers against a handful of screenwriters, within the French cinema of the day
An official ranking of the world's best directors, published every year by *Cahiers du cinéma*
A directing method that Truffaut supposedly codified himself before making his first film
quiz.explication: Truffaut was not drawing up a universal grid: within French cinema in 1954, he was defending filmmakers who wrote their own films against screenwriters he considered dominant. It is Andrew Sarris who, by translating it in 1962, turns it into a general theory, more rigid than the original position.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who formulated, in 1962, the systematized and universal version known as auteur theory?
choix: François Truffaut himself, in a second text published in the United States
André Bazin, Truffaut's mentor at *Cahiers du cinéma*
Andrew Sarris, in the American magazine *Film Culture*
Pauline Kael, in a critical response to Truffaut
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the American critic Andrew Sarris who, eight years after Truffaut's text, translates and systematizes his position into a general theory in *Film Culture*, winter 1962.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Pauline Kael object to in the hardened version of the auteurs policy?
choix: She holds that a film remains a collective work, never the work of one man alone
She judges that Truffaut had no right to borrow a screenplay from Aurenche and Bost
She considers that the Tradition of Quality deserved to be defended more
She objects that Sarris did not cite Truffaut in his text
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pauline Kael attacks the hardened version of the theory by pointing out that a film remains a collective work, never the work of one man alone, even the credited director.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Truffaut back up his attacks on Jean Aurenche and Pierre Bost in his 1954 text?
choix: By citing reviews already published by other *Cahiers* writers
By borrowing one of their screenplays to show, by example, what he held against them
By comparing their adaptations with the eight filmmakers he defends, backed by attendance figures
By publishing excerpts from their private correspondence with André Bazin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Truffaut borrows a screenplay from his two main targets, Aurenche and Bost, to show concretely, by example, what he holds against them in the Tradition of Quality.
